report.source_text: Laboratory tests showed the following: aldolase, 12.7 IU/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 50.9 mm/h; C-reactive protein, 4.76 mg/dL; creatine kinase (CK), 1,081 IU/L; and Krebs von den Lungen (KL)-6, 589 IU/mL (normal range, <499 IU/mL). Results for anti-aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetase, anti-DNA, anti-Jo-1, anti-Scl 70, anti-Sjögren's syndrome-A/B, anti-Sm, and anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein were all negative. Antibodies suggesting immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-signal recognition particle/anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase) were also negative. Anti-centromere antibody was positive. Anti-PM/Scl-75 antibody was qualitatively detected using a line blot assay. Negative results were obtained for anti-PM/Scl-100 antibody. Results for molecular human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing on DNA showed DRB1*01 and DRB1*15.

report.source_text: A muscle biopsy from the left rectus femoris revealed histological findings reflecting active muscle fiber necrosis and regenerative changes (Fig. 2). Reactive mononuclear cell infiltration was seen surrounding necrotic and regenerating fibers. Immunostaining showed the expression of human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-ABC and deposition of membrane attack complex (MAC) on the muscle fiber membranes. Perifascicular atrophy, fibers with internal nuclei, and endomysial fibrosis were not seen. No perivascular collections of inflammatory cells were apparent.

clinician.final_diagnosis: inflammatory myopathy with an apparent clinical classification of PM
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 69-year-old Japanese woman presented with unexplained weight loss and mild, symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness. Initial workup revealed elevated serum creatine kinase (1,081 IU/L) and electromyography showed an abnormal myogenic pattern. Autoantibody testing detected anti-PM/Scl-75 and anti-centromere antibodies, while other common myositis-specific antibodies were negative. A muscle biopsy from the rectus femoris showed active muscle fiber necrosis, regenerative changes, mononuclear cell infiltration, HLA-ABC expression, and membrane attack complex (MAC) deposition. Chest CT showed mild interstitial changes. The myositis was classified as polymyositis (PM) based on criteria by Lundberg et al., noting that the PM subset includes immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM). Treatment with oral prednisolone led to gradual improvement in muscle weakness and normalization of CK levels (211 U/L) before discharge. No recurrence was noted at six months post-discharge.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with mild, symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness and unexplained weight loss.
Serum creatine kinase (CK) was significantly elevated at 1,081 IU/L.
Electromyography (EMG) showed an abnormal myogenic pattern, consistent with myopathy.
Muscle biopsy revealed active muscle fiber necrosis, regenerative changes, mononuclear cell infiltration, HLA-ABC expression, and MAC deposition.
Anti-PM/Scl-75 antibody was qualitatively detected, and anti-centromere antibody was positive.
Chest computed tomography showed mild interstitial changes.
The myositis was classified as PM based on criteria by Lundberg et al., which includes IMNM.
Treatment with oral prednisolone resulted in gradual improvement of muscle weakness and normalization of CK levels.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: No skin lesions (Gottron's lesion, heliotrope rash, mechanic's hands) were evident on physical examination.
No history suggestive of congenital myopathy.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) as a distinct entity
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Antibodies suggesting IMNM (anti-signal recognition particle/anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase) were negative (E001). The final classification statement indicates 'the PM subset includes IMNM' (E008), suggesting it was considered within the broader PM classification rather than a separate diagnosis.

remaining_uncertainties: Specific details of the Lundberg et al. criteria applied and the precise reasoning for classifying it as PM, especially given the biopsy findings (necrosis, MAC deposition) and anti-PM/Scl-75 antibody which can be associated with overlap syndromes or IMNM features.
The extent of comprehensive malignancy screening performed beyond the chest CT, given the unexplained weight loss.
Further details or clinical significance of the mild interstitial changes noted on chest CT.
